glossary.definition: The process of verifying passenger identity, issuing boarding passes, and handling baggage drop-off prior to flight departure.
The coordinated process of managing passenger entry onto the aircraft according to boarding procedures and groups.
The management of passenger luggage throughout its journey from check-in to aircraft loading, transfer, and claim.
All activities conducted on the ground that support and enable aircraft operations, excluding flight itself.
The process of preparing an aircraft for its next flight after arrival, including cleaning, refueling, and servicing.
The planning of flight routes, fuel loads, and operational decisions related to the safe and efficient execution of a flight.
The activities of the Operations Control Center in centrally monitoring and coordinating flights and operational decisions.
The scheduling, assignment, and administration of flight crew and cabin crew across airline operations.
A systematic approach to managing safety risks, including policies, procedures, and processes for ensuring aviation safety.
The scheduling and oversight of aircraft maintenance activities to ensure airworthiness and regulatory compliance.
The procedures and measures implemented to protect passengers, crew, aircraft, and airport facilities from security threats.
The handling of flight schedule impacts and operational adjustments caused by adverse weather conditions.
The processes for managing and mitigating the effects of flight delays and cancellations on passengers and operations.
The predefined procedures and actions taken by airline and airport personnel during emergency situations.
The handling, transport, and regulatory compliance of hazardous materials carried on aircraft.
The programs for staff training and adherence to aviation regulatory standards and internal policies.

A comprehensive reference document that codifies airline operational procedures, safety principles, governance practices, and industry-standard workflows to support operational personnel, training, and decision-making.
Established procedural frameworks outlining approved methods for conducting airline and ground operations, used to ensure consistency, safety, and regulatory compliance.
The regulatory concept and framework governing the authority and responsibility for managing the safe initiation, continuation, and termination of flight operations.
A systematic approach to managing aviation safety, encompassing safety principles, risk mitigation, and governance practices published by recognized aviation safety authorities.
The overarching framework and discipline that integrates operational procedures, ground operations, safety management, and governance to coordinate airline activities.
Tools, systems, and knowledge resources used by airline operational personnel to inform and assist operational decision-making, including AI-powered assistants and procedural references.
Standards governing the classification, documentation, handling, and transport of hazardous materials in airline operations.
Standardized industry practices for managing aircraft, passengers, baggage, and cargo at airport facilities.
A comprehensive document that outlines an airline's operational procedures, policies, and standards for safe and efficient operations.
Standardized procedures established for conducting safe, efficient, compliant, and customer-focused airline operations.
Operational principle that safety takes precedence over operational efficiency, schedule performance, commercial objectives, and financial considerations.
Adherence to national aviation regulations, airport authority requirements, ATC instructions, company operating procedures, and aircraft manufacturer guidance.
Directives issued by air traffic control that all airline operations must comply with.
Operational and regulatory requirements imposed by airport authorities that airline operations must satisfy.
Ongoing process of periodically reviewing operational procedures to identify safety improvements, efficiency opportunities, training requirements, and technology enhancements.
Top-level organizational leadership responsible for corporate strategy, regulatory oversight, financial management, and safety policy approval.
Organizational unit within the airline structure dedicated to the execution and management of operational activities.
An operational principle stating that safety shall take precedence over operational efficiency, schedule performance, commercial objectives, and financial considerations.
The organizational division responsible for aircraft turnaround, ramp operations, passenger handling, and baggage handling.
The organizational division responsible for maintenance, airworthiness, engineering support, and aircraft reliability.
The organizational unit responsible for risk management, safety investigations, compliance monitoring, and safety reporting.
Activities conducted on the airport ramp area, including servicing and preparing aircraft between flights.
The management and processing of passengers at the airport, including check-in, boarding, and arrival procedures.
The condition of an aircraft being fit and safe for flight, maintained by the technical operations division.
The function of planning, monitoring, and managing flight operations including flight plan release and in-flight support.
The dependability and consistent performance of aircraft, monitored by the technical operations division.
Organizational division responsible for daily flight operations, crew management, dispatch, and operational control of an airline.
Central coordination hub for airline operations that maintains continuous situational awareness of aircraft locations, flight status, weather, airport conditions, and crew availability.
Event that interferes with normal airline operations, managed through coordinated interdepartmental and OCC activities.
The process of tracking all flights from departure until arrival, including departure times, arrival times, route deviations, fuel status, and aircraft performance.
The management of operational disruptions including delays, diversions, cancellations, aircraft substitutions, and crew reassignments.
The replacement of one aircraft with another as part of managing operational disruptions.
The reassignment of crew members as part of managing operational disruptions.
A monitored event in which a flight deviates from its planned route.
A process conducted by the Safety Manager to evaluate safety risks.
An investigation coordinated by the Safety Manager following a safety event.
Operations Control Center — the organizational unit responsible for tracking flights, managing disruptions, and maintaining communication across operational stakeholders.
The redirection of a flight to an airport other than its planned destination, managed as part of disruption management.
The set of conditions that must be satisfied before a flight may be dispatched, covering aircraft, crew, environmental, and airport requirements.
Dispatch prerequisites relating to the aircraft, including airworthiness, absence of unresolved critical defects, and conformance with operational requirements.
The condition of an aircraft being in a state safe and compliant with regulatory standards for flight operations.
Dispatch prerequisites relating to assigned crew, including qualification, medical fitness, duty time compliance, and required certifications.
Dispatch prerequisites relating to departure and destination airports, including operational status, performance capability, and support for planned operations.
Dispatch prerequisites relating to weather, requiring that conditions meet operational minima and do not create unacceptable risk.
The structured hierarchy through which operational decisions are escalated and resolved, starting from routine operations.
Level 1 in the operational decision-making hierarchy, encompassing minor issues such as gate changes, minor delays, and passenger accommodations, handled by operational personnel.
Minimum weather and environmental conditions that must be satisfied to safely conduct flight operations.
Regulations governing the maximum working hours and minimum rest periods for assigned crew members.
Level 2 disruptions such as significant delays, equipment failures, or crew shortages, handled by supervisors.
Level 3 serious events such as airport closures, severe weather, or aircraft grounding, managed by OCC management.
Level 4 severe events such as major accidents, security incidents, or national emergencies, handled by executive management.
Procedures ensuring operational documents are version controlled, annually reviewed, approved before publication, and distributed to affected personnel.
A major disruption event that renders an airport unavailable for operations, requiring OCC management involvement.
A major disruption event involving the removal of aircraft from service, requiring OCC management oversight.
An operational flight record authorizing a flight to depart under specified conditions.
An operational record documenting the cause and circumstances of flight delays.
Maintenance records that confirm an aircraft meets regulatory standards for safe operation.
A safety record documenting identified hazards to operations or personnel.
A safety record documenting incidents that occur during operations for review and investigation.
Crew records documenting the certifications, licenses, and competencies of operating personnel.
A crew record documenting the periods of duty and rest for flight personnel.
A formal process requiring personnel to immediately escalate safety concerns, regulatory violations, security incidents, and emergencies through the established chain of command.
The hierarchical reporting structure through which operational issues and emergencies are escalated.
The systematic retention of operational records, including flight, crew, maintenance, and safety records, according to regulatory requirements.
A structured process for implementing operational changes that includes risk assessment, stakeholder identification, documentation updates, personnel training, and monitoring of results.
The operational function ensuring the safe, efficient, secure, and customer-focused movement of passengers from check-in through to arrival at their destination.
The initial stage of the passenger journey at the airport where passengers register for their flight and begin the departure process.
The coordination of all stages a passenger experiences from reservation support through check-in, boarding, arrival assistance, and connection support.
The process of confirming that passenger travel documents are present, valid, and compliant with regulatory requirements prior to acceptance for travel.
The handling and processing of passenger baggage during check-in as part of the passenger journey.
A document issued to passengers during check-in that authorizes them to board the aircraft.
Assistance provided to passengers transferring between flights to ensure smooth continuation of their journey.
Identified passenger needs identified during check-in that require additional accommodation or assistance during the journey.
Coordination activities undertaken during the passenger journey to satisfy applicable security requirements.
Determination that a passenger possesses valid, non-expired, and compliant travel documents and may be accepted for travel.
The process of assigning passenger seats based on aircraft configuration, preferences, safety requirements, special assistance needs, and operational considerations.
Seating in emergency exit rows that may only be assigned to passengers meeting applicable eligibility requirements, excluding those requiring special assistance.
Documentation and regulatory conditions that must be satisfied by passengers connecting through intermediate destinations on international travel.
Visa documentation that must be verified as part of international travel document checks prior to passenger acceptance.
Accommodation criteria for passengers with disabilities or special needs, which influence seat assignment and exclude them from emergency exit rows.
Baggage accepted into the aircraft hold only after passenger verification, flight verification, weight verification, and security screening.
Identification labels applied to baggage during acceptance to track ownership and destination routing.
Coding system applied to baggage tags to confirm routing to the correct destination.
Non-standard baggage categories including sporting equipment, musical instruments, medical devices, mobility aids, oversized baggage, and fragile items requiring special tagging and handling.
Charges collected for baggage exceeding company policy allowances.

Screening process performed by Passenger Services personnel to identify prohibited and restricted items such as lithium batteries, flammable materials, explosives, compressed gases, and corrosive substances before baggage acceptance.
Items such as lithium batteries, flammable materials, explosives, compressed gases, and corrosive substances that are restricted or banned from baggage acceptance.
Security check requirement that must be satisfied as a prerequisite for accepting checked baggage.
A label applied to checked baggage to identify ownership, confirm destination coding, and track the item through the handling system.

Services provided to passengers requiring additional support, including those with reduced mobility, elderly passengers, passengers with medical conditions, and visually or hearing impaired passengers.

Coordinated assistance for passengers needing wheelchairs from check-in through final arrival, ensuring proper documentation, equipment availability, and safe transportation through airport facilities.
Equipment such as wheelchairs and mobility aids required by passengers, which must not be separated from the passenger without approved procedures.
Preferential boarding granted to passengers requiring special assistance, such as those needing wheelchair services, where appropriate.
Children traveling without a guardian, accepted only in accordance with company policy and subject to verification of guardian information.
Any suspected violation of dangerous goods regulations that must be immediately reported by personnel.
Passengers requiring additional support, including those with reduced mobility, elderly, medical conditions, or visual/hearing impairments.
Coordinated service providing wheelchair support from check-in through final arrival, including equipment availability and safe transport.
A child traveling without a guardian, accepted only per company policy with required documentation and supervision throughout the journey.
Evaluation process applied to passengers with medical requirements to determine fitness and needs prior to travel.
Approval process for medical equipment such as oxygen arrangements brought aboard by passengers with medical needs.
Priority passengers such as government officials, corporate executives, frequent flyers, or special guests entitled to expedited processing.
Support provided to passengers with reduced mobility to facilitate airport processing and boarding.
The requirement that an unaccompanied or young child remains under airline personnel supervision throughout airport processing until transferred to authorized personnel at destination.
Pre-gate-closure steps including completion of final passenger counts and readiness checks before departure.
The point at which the boarding gate is closed and no further passengers may board without explicit approval.
The process of verifying that all boarded passengers match the passenger manifests, boarding records, and security records prior to departure.
The refusal to allow a passenger to board due to overbooking, documentation deficiencies, security concerns, or operational restrictions.
Situations in which a passenger fails to make a connecting flight, triggering airline assistance such as rebooking, accommodation, meal vouchers, or transportation arrangements.
The boarding-stage verification that ensures all passengers have cleared security and are accounted for against security records.
A document listing all passengers booked on a flight, used as the reference during passenger reconciliation.
The practice of selling more tickets than available seats, which may result in denied boarding for some passengers.
The coordinated set of actions taken during a flight delay, including providing updates, managing expectations, coordinating support services, and escalating passenger concerns.
The procedures triggered when a flight is cancelled, encompassing prompt passenger notification, rebooking, coordination of support services, and application of compensation policies.

The procedures executed upon aircraft arrival, including disembarkation coordination, priority support for passengers requiring special assistance, guidance for transfer passengers, and arrival information communication.
The process of receiving, handling, and resolving customer complaints in a professional and respectful manner.
Measures used to restore customer confidence after service failures, including rebooking assistance, travel credits, meal vouchers, hotel accommodations, and transportation support.
Safety-related duties of passenger services personnel, including supporting safety announcements, emergency procedures, evacuation readiness, and security compliance.
Ongoing assessment of passenger services performance to ensure service quality and identify areas for improvement.
Procedures for rebooking passengers following flight cancellations or disruptions, initiated immediately upon cancellation.
Passengers connecting from an arriving flight to another flight, who receive guidance during arrival operations.
Compensation in the form of credits for future travel, offered as part of service recovery measures.
Vouchers provided to passengers for meals during service disruptions as part of service recovery.
Lodging arrangements provided to passengers as a service recovery measure during disruptions.
Transport arrangements provided to passengers as a service recovery measure, such as ground transportation during disruptions.
State of preparedness supported by passenger services personnel for emergency evacuation of the aircraft.
Process of reviewing customer complaints to identify recurring issues and improvement opportunities for passenger service delivery.
Performance metric measuring how quickly and smoothly passengers are processed and loaded onto the aircraft.
Adherence to regulatory and airline security requirements during passenger handling and check-in operations.
Standardized processes for passenger check-in applicable across all flight types and check-in channels including counters, kiosks, online, mobile, and off-airport facilities.
Pre-opening verification steps that passenger service personnel must perform, including system, printer, and supply checks plus a supervisor-led briefing before check-in begins.
Confirmation that systems, printers, baggage tag stock, boarding pass stock, manifests, schedules, seat maps, notices, and communication systems are functioning before counter operations commence.
Pre-shift briefing conducted by counter supervisors covering passenger loads, special assistance needs, operational disruptions, weather, security alerts, staffing, and flight-specific information.

Process of validating passenger identity against approved government-issued documentation, requiring exact match of names with reservation records and resolution of any discrepancies before completion.
A flight marketed and sold under one airline's designator but operated by another carrier, covered under the same check-in procedures as other services.
Forms of identification deemed valid for airline travel, including passports, national identity cards, and government-issued ID cards.
The process of evaluating expired or damaged identification documents according to applicable regulations and airline policy.
Any suspected fraudulent travel documentation, which must be immediately reported to supervisory personnel and airport security authorities.
The procedure of verifying and confirming the validity of an airline reservation as part of the check-in/boarding process.
The verification of whether a passenger meets the requirements necessary to travel, conducted during check-in operations.
The maintenance of on-time performance and operational reliability of flights, which check-in operations help support.
Official documents issued to passengers during check-in to authorize and facilitate their travel.
A passenger without a confirmed seat who is processed according to standby procedures pending seat availability.
A passenger on a waitlist who may only be assigned a confirmed seat when authorized by operational systems and applicable company policies.
Verification of passport validity, visa, transit, health, immigration, customs, and destination-specific entry conditions required for international travel.
Approval granted to a passenger for travel after reservation and documentation verification, including escalation of any discrepancies.
The issuance of a boarding pass only after documentation deficiencies have been identified and resolved.
Requirements that passengers must meet to be assigned to emergency exit row seats, including physical capability to assist in an emergency, understanding of instructions, and regulatory compliance.
Seating assignment considerations for passengers requiring special assistance, who are prohibited from being assigned to emergency exit row seats.
Weight and balance distribution requirements that must be considered when assigning passenger seats to maintain proper aircraft stability.
Service benefits and rights associated with premium cabin or class tickets that influence seat assignment decisions.
The process of assigning passengers to specific seats, taking into account preferences, operational needs, aircraft balance, accessibility requirements, premium entitlements, and safety restrictions.
The procedure of confirming that a passenger is authorized and compliant to travel, including adherence to security and regulatory requirements.
The handling, acceptance, and routing of passenger baggage as part of the check-in workflow.
The act of generating and providing tickets, boarding passes, and other required travel documents to passengers during check-in.
A performance indicator measuring how successfully the airline resolves passenger complaints and service failures.
Adherence to regulatory requirements, security protocols, and internal operational standards governing passenger handling.
Ongoing programs driven by regular review of operational performance data to enhance service quality and efficiency.
A document issued to passengers that they must retain as proof of checked baggage until it is successfully recovered at destination.
Additional fees collected from passengers when baggage exceeds applicable weight or size restrictions.
Maximum weight restrictions applied to checked baggage, with non-compliant baggage requiring authorization or rejection for safety reasons.
Baggage exceeding standard dimensions that requires special handling procedures and may incur additional charges.
Operational systems used to record and monitor checked baggage throughout handling and transport to ensure traceability.
Items such as lithium batteries, compressed gases, and hazardous chemicals that require special review before transport.
Passengers requiring additional services during their journey, including those with reduced mobility, sensory impairments, medical needs, or language requirements.
A special assistance category for passengers with mobility limitations who require documented services coordinated throughout the passenger journey.
Approved procedure for handling minors traveling alone, requiring verification of guardian information, emergency contacts, identification, and authorization documentation before acceptance.
Requirement that unaccompanied minors remain under staff supervision until transferred to authorized personnel at the destination.
The process by which personnel confirm that baggage being checked belongs to the passenger presenting it.
Operational systems used to record and monitor checked baggage as it moves through the airline's handling process.
Baggage exceeding the standard weight limit, processed according to approved procedures and subject to additional charges.
Tags applied to special baggage to communicate specific handling requirements to baggage operations personnel.
Restrictions on the airline's liability for special baggage, which passengers must be advised of along with applicable handling restrictions.
The process of confirming a passenger's identity and travel authorization before services such as check-in or baggage acceptance are provided.
A tag applied to checked baggage indicating its destination and routing information.
A system used to record and track baggage through the handling and transportation process.
An additional fee collected from passengers when baggage exceeds applicable weight or size limitations.
Additional handling instructions applied to special baggage, communicated via tags and to baggage operations personnel.
An assessment of a passenger's medical condition to determine whether they are physically able to undertake travel, referred to designated authorities when concerns arise.
A procedure for efficiently processing multiple passengers together while maintaining individual passenger verification and accountability.
The published cut-off time after which arriving passengers may be denied acceptance depending on operational conditions.
The processing of passengers arriving after the published check-in deadline, subject to evaluation of time, baggage, security, and boarding constraints.
Operational disruption during check-in, including delays, cancellations, gate changes, aircraft substitutions, weather events, maintenance issues, and security concerns.
The provision of timely, accurate, factual, and professional information to passengers during operational disruptions, consistent with approved operational information.
The procedure for closing check-in operations according to published schedules, including verification of passenger counts, baggage, standby, and special assistance status.
The handling and verification of standby passengers as part of check-in closure procedures prior to flight departure.
The verification of baggage status as part of the check-in closure procedure before flight departure.
Ongoing monitoring of check-in performance through operational audits, customer feedback, compliance reviews, and performance metrics to drive continuous improvement.
Quantitative measures used to monitor departure on-time performance and related operational outcomes during check-in.
Requests for special accommodations or services made by passengers, reviewed during pre-boarding preparation to ensure appropriate handling.
Systematic reviews of operational processes used to monitor check-in performance, compliance, and service quality.
Activities conducted prior to boarding commencement to verify operational readiness, including reviewing manifests, security requirements, and special service requests.
Procedures to ensure boarding equipment, scanners, public announcement systems, and passenger information displays are operational before passenger arrival at the gate.
Devices used at the gate to scan boarding passes and verify passenger eligibility to board the aircraft.
Passengers transferring from one flight to another as part of their journey, subject to standard boarding procedures.
Flights on which passengers continue their journey at an intermediate point, governed by standard boarding procedures.
Non-scheduled flight services operated for specific groups or purposes, subject to standard boarding procedures.
Standardized processes governing passenger boarding across all flight types, including scheduled, charter, repositioning, and special operations flights.
Pre-boarding examination of the passenger list by gate personnel to verify counts and identify special categories such as VIPs, unaccompanied minors, and standby passengers.
Process of identifying and coordinating with airport assistance personnel for passengers requiring wheelchair, medical, or mobility support before boarding commences.
Passengers without confirmed seats who wait for availability and are tracked on the passenger manifest.
Very important persons identified on the passenger manifest who may require prioritized or special handling during boarding.
Airline crew members traveling as passengers rather than working positions, tracked on the boarding manifest.
Notifications attached to passenger records flagging individuals requiring additional security screening or attention before boarding.
Physical equipment such as jet bridges, boarding ramps, and related apparatus used to facilitate passenger boarding at the gate.
An airline crew member traveling as a passenger rather than in an operational duty position, listed on the passenger manifest.
Public communications issued at the gate providing passengers with boarding sequence, gate information, requirements, and carry-on restrictions.
Rules governing the size, type, and quantity of items passengers may bring into the aircraft cabin, communicated during boarding announcements.
The ordered method by which passengers are permitted to enter the aircraft, organized into approved boarding groups.
Organizational categories used to manage the boarding order, structured by cabin class, loyalty status, seat location, or special assistance needs.
The organized process of boarding passengers according to approved boarding groups, which may be structured by cabin class, loyalty status, seat location, or operational needs.
The gate process of validating a passenger's boarding pass by confirming identity, flight number, departure date, boarding authorization, and seat assignment before allowing access to the aircraft.
Security procedure ensuring that the passenger's identity matches boarding documentation and that all travel documents are valid and meet applicable security requirements.
Gate-level monitoring to ensure carry-on baggage meets airline size, weight, and content restrictions before passengers board the aircraft.
Procedure for clearing standby passengers only after available seating capacity is confirmed, including seat assignment, manifest updates, and boarding authorization.
Procedures for handling overbooked flights by prioritizing voluntary solutions, rebooking options, and customer service recovery measures.
Approved procedures for managing situations of involuntary denied boarding in accordance with regulatory requirements and company policy.
Requirements for carry-on items to meet size limits, weight limitations, and security restrictions; excess items may be transferred to checked baggage if operationally necessary.
Approved procedure applied to passengers involuntarily denied boarding on overbooked flights, executed in accordance with regulatory requirements and company policy.
Final point at which the boarding process is terminated; standby boarding should be completed before this moment whenever possible.
A passenger who fails to report for boarding before closure, triggering contact attempts, status verification, operational record updates, and associated baggage security handling.
Authorization to depart the aircraft, granted only after all reconciliation discrepancies have been resolved.
The last boarding announcement made per operational schedules, identifying remaining passengers, boarding closure deadlines, and consequences of missed boarding.
The process by which gate personnel communicate boarding status, passenger count, special assistance status, and boarding completion time to flight crew, ground operations, and dispatch.
The recorded time at which boarding concludes, communicated as part of aircraft communications to relevant operational personnel.
The verification that the passenger manifest correctly reflects all passengers expected and processed for the flight.
The transmission of boarding progress information from gate personnel to flight crew, ground operations, operations control center, and dispatch personnel.
Information regarding passengers requiring special assistance that must be communicated as part of boarding status updates.
The completion of passenger counts, manifest updates, boarding reports, and irregularity documentation after boarding has finished.
A disruption to the scheduled boarding process requiring cause identification, accurate communication, corrective action coordination, and escalation of significant disruptions.
An unexpected occurrence during boarding such as aircraft substitutions, gate changes, security incidents, passenger disturbances, system failures, or weather disruptions.
An alteration to the assigned departure gate, managed as an irregular boarding event with continuous stakeholder communication.
Disruptions to the boarding process requiring personnel to identify causes, communicate accurate information, coordinate corrective actions, and provide timely passenger updates.

Unexpected occurrences during boarding such as aircraft substitutions, gate changes, security incidents, passenger disturbances, system failures, or weather disruptions, addressed through approved contingency procedures.
Approved response actions followed by personnel when irregular boarding events occur, ensuring continuous communication with operational stakeholders.
Passenger list that must be finalized and updated as part of post-boarding documentation.
Documentation of boarding activities retained according to company requirements, including reports and recorded irregularities.
Disruptive, aggressive, intoxicated, or threatening passenger behavior during boarding that requires safety risk assessment and possible denial of boarding.
Permission to board granted only after passengers have been evaluated for safety and security risks.
A quality assurance metric ensuring passenger counts are correctly matched against manifests.
A quality assurance metric tracking the punctuality of flight departures relative to scheduled times.
Procedures ensuring the safe, secure, accurate, and timely movement of passenger baggage from acceptance through delivery in compliance with safety and security regulations.
Baggage requiring transfer routing between flights as part of its journey to the final destination.
Baggage that has not arrived at its intended destination within expected timeframes and is subject to mishandling procedures.
Baggage subject to processing errors, including misrouting, loss, or incorrect delivery, addressed within baggage handling procedures.
The assignment of a unique baggage identification number to each item, recorded in approved baggage tracking systems and verified against passenger reservation records.
Required pre-loading screening of all baggage, which may include X-ray inspection, explosive detection screening, manual inspection, or additional procedures mandated by local authorities.
The process of sorting baggage by destination, flight number, transfer routing, and handling requirements after acceptance and security screening.
Baggage designated with priority status during sorting operations to ensure expedited handling.
Baggage belonging to airline crew members, included within the scope of baggage handling procedures.

Procedures for handling baggage continuing onto a connecting flight, including verification of onward flight information, confirmation of routing, meeting transfer deadlines, and coordination with connecting stations.
Transfer baggage with tight connection times that receives priority handling to minimize transfer failures.
Time limits by which transfer baggage must be processed to make onward connections.
Baggage belonging to passengers traveling in premium cabins, designated for priority handling.
Baggage belonging to frequent flyer program members, designated for priority handling.
Baggage flagged for operational reasons to receive expedited handling and loading.
Baggage containing delicate items such as musical instruments, electronics, artwork, or glass, requiring tagged special handling.
Wheelchairs and mobility devices that receive special handling, including condition recording, component protection, and prioritized delivery on arrival.
The process of loading baggage onto an aircraft in compliance with weight and balance requirements, load control instructions, compartment limitations, and special handling needs.
Coordination with load control personnel to ensure baggage distribution meets aircraft operational requirements, with discrepancies reported immediately and loading halted until corrected.
Safe baggage loading practices including proper lifting techniques, use of approved equipment, compliance with ramp safety rules, and awareness of moving vehicles.
Operational requirements that baggage loading must support to ensure proper aircraft weight distribution and performance.
Instructions and personnel coordination responsible for managing aircraft loading, including baggage distribution and operational compliance.
Constraints on baggage compartments that loading activities must respect to avoid affecting aircraft performance.
Additional handling requirements applicable to specific types of baggage, such as mobility and medical equipment.
Coordination of baggage placement across the aircraft to meet weight, balance, and operational requirements.
Safety rules governing operations on the airport ramp area, including awareness of moving vehicles.
Special handling of mobility aids and equipment, which shall be treated with the same level of care as medical equipment.
Pre-departure confirmation that baggage loaded onto the aircraft corresponds to accepted passengers, verifying passenger status, counts, and security requirements.
Procedures for identifying, verifying, and potentially removing baggage associated with passengers who fail to board, completed before departure.
Approved procedures for unloading baggage upon aircraft arrival, prioritizing mobility aids.
Procedures for identifying and handling baggage associated with passengers who fail to board, including locating affected baggage and removing it if required by security rules.
Delivery of baggage to passengers ensuring correct destination delivery, accurate carousel assignment, and timely passenger communication.
Classification of baggage as lost when recovery efforts fail within established timelines, prompting tracing investigations.
Report created when baggage is delayed, used to verify passenger information, initiate tracing, and provide updates to the passenger.
Investigation process initiated to locate and reunite delayed or lost baggage with its owner.
Baggage handled under normal processing and delivery procedures without priority or transfer requirements.
Standard procedures followed when baggage is classified as lost after recovery efforts fail within established timelines.
Procedures for inspecting, documenting, and assessing compensation for passenger-reported baggage damage.
Baggage remaining unclaimed after arrival, transferred to designated storage facilities for owner verification and contact.
The mandatory documentation of baggage-related events including loss, damage, and irregularities.
The allocation of specific baggage carousels at arrival areas for accurate delivery to passengers.
Monitoring of baggage handling performance using metrics such as mishandled baggage rates, delivery times, damage rates, transfer success rates, and complaint trends.
Assessment of whether a passenger qualifies for compensation following a baggage-related incident, conducted per applicable regulations and company policy.
A performance metric measuring the frequency of baggage handling errors relative to total baggage processed, used to evaluate operational quality.
Documentation maintained for unclaimed baggage placed in designated storage facilities, including ownership verification and contact attempt logs.
An approved system used to monitor baggage throughout its journey, supporting acceptance, routing, loading, arrival, and delivery confirmation records.
A report documenting baggage-related incidents such as delays, damage, security incidents, mishandling, or tracking failures, reviewed to identify recurring operational issues.
A performance indicator measuring the rate of successful baggage transfers between flights, used in baggage handling performance monitoring.
A performance metric measuring the rate at which baggage is damaged, monitored as part of baggage handling performance evaluation.
A performance metric used to measure adherence to security requirements in baggage handling operations.
The designated location at an airport where an aircraft is parked, marking the start and end points of ground operations activities.
Activities performed on the ground in support of aircraft operations, which personnel must execute in compliance with approved operational procedures, safety requirements, and security regulations.
The process by which ground personnel guide an arriving aircraft to its designated parking position using approved hand signals or a docking guidance system.
Approved systems used to assist marshalling personnel in accurately guiding aircraft into the designated parking position at the gate.
Any loose material or contamination found during inspection of aircraft parking stands that could pose a hazard to aircraft or personnel.
Wedge-shaped blocks installed against an aircraft's wheels after parking to prevent unintended movement.
Verification that an aircraft's engines are fully shut down before ground personnel or equipment are permitted to approach the aircraft.
Ground operations involving the use of equipment to push an aircraft back from the gate as part of departure preparation.
Designated restricted areas established around parked aircraft to protect personnel from hazards during ground operations.
Restricted areas around aircraft engines where personnel exposure poses a risk of injury.
Restricted zones around propeller blades where personnel must not enter due to rotating blade dangers.
Areas behind jet aircraft where exhaust thrust creates hazardous conditions for ground personnel.
Restricted areas around aircraft during refueling operations where safety conditions must be maintained.
Designated routes used for the movement of aircraft on the ground, marked as restricted for personnel.
Required approval that must be granted before ground personnel may approach an aircraft, contingent on safety conditions being satisfied.
The process of passengers leaving the aircraft after arrival, requiring safe positioning of equipment such as jet bridges and stairs and coordination with cabin crew.
Equipment used in ground handling operations, including passenger stairs, belt loaders, pushback tractors, ground power units, air conditioning units, baggage carts, tow bars, and service vehicles.
Operational zones within ground operations where unauthorized personnel are prohibited from entering.
Procedures following aircraft arrival for safely positioning equipment such as jet bridges, stairs, and mobility assistance devices, and coordinating with cabin crew for orderly passenger movement.
A ground support vehicle used to push aircraft back from the gate when they cannot reverse under their own power.
Devices inspected and used during passenger disembarkation to assist passengers requiring mobility support.
Procedures for unloading baggage from arriving aircraft only after safety procedures are complete, following approved loading plans and handling requirements.
Procedures for unloading, transferring, and loading cargo and mail shipments, including verification of documentation, handling requirements, security status, and destination information.
Post-disembarkation activities including waste removal, cleaning of seating areas and lavatories, replenishing cabin supplies, and inspecting cabin condition within turnaround timelines.
Accelerated handling applied to priority, mobility, transfer, and special baggage to ensure timely delivery to designated processing areas.
Approved plans that dictate how baggage is to be loaded and unloaded according to handling requirements.
The unloading, transferring, and loading of cargo shipments according to approved procedures, including verification of documentation, handling requirements, security status, and destination.
The processing of mail shipments involving verification of documentation, handling requirements, security status, and destination information.
Documents verified by personnel during cargo and mail handling to confirm handling requirements, security status, and destination information.
Cargo categories requiring additional controls, handled according to applicable regulations and company procedures.
Operations performed after passenger disembarkation and safety clearance, including waste removal, seating and lavatory cleaning, and cabin supply replenishment.
Scheduled timeframes within which cleaning activities must be completed while maintaining quality standards.
Aircraft servicing activity that refills the onboard water supply using approved equipment while following hygiene and contamination prevention requirements.
Aircraft servicing activity involving the removal of lavatory waste, performed with approved equipment and in compliance with environmental and health regulations.
Coordinated delivery and loading of food, beverages, and service supplies, including removal of used supplies, inventory verification, and documentation.

Aircraft refueling conducted only by authorized personnel, requiring completed grounding procedures, verified fire safety requirements, confirmed fuel quantities, and established communication channels.
Safety prerequisites verified prior to fueling operations to ensure fire hazards are controlled during aircraft refueling.
Maintenance action taken to correct or resolve reported aircraft defects discovered during or prior to turnaround.
Maintenance activity involving systematic evaluation of aircraft systems and components to ensure continued airworthiness during turnaround.
The period during which an aircraft is prepared between arrival and departure, encompassing all servicing, maintenance, and loading activities.
Monitoring and management by turnaround coordinators of all servicing activities to ensure completion within scheduled timelines, with delay communication to operational control.
